title: Introduction to Excretion
content:
# Introduction to Excretion

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Define excretion and explain why it is necessary
- Identify the main excretory products and organs
- Distinguish between excretion and egestion
- Understand the importance of removing waste products

## Introduction

**Excretion** is the removal of metabolic waste products from the body. These wastes are produced by chemical reactions inside cells and must be removed because they are toxic if they accumulate. Excretion is essential for maintaining a stable internal environment.

## Key Concepts

### What is Excretion?

**Definition:** The removal of metabolic waste products and excess substances from the body

**Key points:**
- Waste products are made inside cells
- They result from metabolism
- They would be toxic if allowed to build up
- Different organs excrete different wastes

### Excretion vs Egestion

| Process | Definition | Example |
|---------|------------|----------|
| Excretion | Removal of metabolic waste | CO₂ from respiration |
| Egestion | Removal of undigested food | Faeces |

**Important:** Faeces are NOT excretory products - the material was never inside cells!

### Main Excretory Products

| Waste product | Produced from | Toxic if accumulated | Excreted by |
|---------------|---------------|---------------------|-------------|
| Carbon dioxide | Respiration | Yes (acidic) | Lungs |
| Urea | Protein breakdown | Yes | Kidneys |
| Excess water | Various processes | No (but causes problems) | Kidneys |
| Excess salts | Diet | No (but causes problems) | Kidneys |

### Carbon Dioxide

**Produced by:** Aerobic respiration in all cells

$$\text{Glucose} + \text{Oxygen} \rightarrow \text{Carbon dioxide} + \text{Water}$$

**Why it must be removed:**
- Dissolves in blood forming carbonic acid
- Makes blood too acidic
- Affects enzyme function
- Disrupts homeostasis

**Excreted by:** Lungs (breathing out)

### Urea

**Produced from:** Excess amino acids (from protein digestion)

**Where formed:** Liver (deamination)

**Process:**
$$\text{Amino acid} \xrightarrow{\text{liver}} \text{Ammonia} + \text{Carbohydrate part}$$
$$\text{Ammonia} + \text{CO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{liver}} \text{Urea}$$

**Why it must be removed:**
- Urea is toxic in high concentrations
- Cannot store excess protein
- Ammonia is even more toxic

**Excreted by:** Kidneys (in urine)

### Deamination

**Definition:** Removal of amino group from amino acids

**Location:** Liver

**Why necessary:**
- Excess amino acids cannot be stored
- Amino group contains nitrogen
- Nitrogen must be removed

**Products:**
- Ammonia (converted to urea)
- Remainder used for respiration or converted to fat

### Excretory Organs

| Organ | What it excretes |
|-------|------------------|
| Lungs | Carbon dioxide, water vapour |
| Kidneys | Urea, excess water, excess salts |
| Skin | Small amounts of urea, water, salts (sweat) |

### The Lungs

**Excrete:**
- Carbon dioxide (main excretory function)
- Water vapour

**Process:**
1. CO₂ produced by respiration in cells
2. Dissolves in blood plasma
3. Transported to lungs
4. Diffuses into alveoli
5. Breathed out

### The Kidneys

**Excrete:**
- Urea (main function)
- Excess water
- Excess salts

**Also regulate:**
- Water balance
- Ion balance
- Blood pH

### The Skin

**Through sweat:**
- Small amount of urea
- Water
- Salts

**Note:** Sweating is primarily for temperature regulation, not excretion

### Why is Excretion Important?

| If waste accumulates | Effect |
|---------------------|--------|
| Too much CO₂ | Blood becomes acidic; enzymes affected |
| Too much urea | Toxic; damages cells |
| Too much water | Cells swell; may burst |
| Too little water | Cells shrink; enzymes affected |
| Wrong salt balance | Nerve and muscle function affected |

### Links to Other Systems

| System | Link to excretion |
|--------|-------------------|
| Circulatory | Transports wastes to excretory organs |
| Respiratory | Excretes CO₂ |
| Digestive | Liver makes urea |
| Urinary | Kidneys excrete urea |

## Common Exam Questions

- Define excretion
- Name the main excretory products and organs
- Explain the difference between excretion and egestion
- Explain why excretion is necessary

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** Faeces are excretory products
- **Reality:** Faeces are egested, not excreted

- **Misconception:** Sweating is mainly for excretion
- **Reality:** Sweating is mainly for temperature regulation

- **Misconception:** We only excrete when we go to the toilet
- **Reality:** We excrete CO₂ with every breath

- **Misconception:** All carbon dioxide comes from the lungs
- **Reality:** CO₂ is produced by all cells; lungs just excrete it

## Practice Questions

1. Define excretion. (2 marks)

2. State two excretory products and name the organs that excrete them. (2 marks)

3. Explain the difference between excretion and egestion. (2 marks)

4. Explain why carbon dioxide must be removed from the body. (3 marks)

5. Describe how urea is formed from excess amino acids. (3 marks)

6. Explain why excretion is essential for maintaining a stable internal environment. Include reference to specific waste products. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Excretion | Removal of metabolic waste products |
| Egestion | Removal of undigested food |
| Metabolic waste | Substance produced by chemical reactions in cells |
| Urea | Nitrogenous waste from protein breakdown |
| Deamination | Removal of amino group from amino acids |
| Homeostasis | Maintaining a stable internal environment |

## Summary

- Excretion removes metabolic waste products from the body
- Different from egestion (removing undigested food)
- Main wastes: CO₂ (from respiration) and urea (from protein breakdown)
- CO₂ excreted by lungs; urea by kidneys
- Urea made in liver from excess amino acids (deamination)
- Excretion essential to prevent toxic build-up
- Also involves removing excess water and salts
